title: Atomistic Structure Generation and Neural-Network Screening of Hard Carbons to Identify High-Capacity Sodium Storage
authors: Harry Mclean, Aiden Daniel Emery, Theodore Thomas Walton, Ned Thaddeus Taylor, Steven Paul Hepplestone
abstract: Hard carbons are established anodes for lithium-ion batteries and leading candidates for sodium-ion batteries, yet their electrochemical performance is governed by a heterogeneous network of graphitic domains, defects, and nanopores that conventional atomistic methods cannot model at the required length scales. We combine universal machine-learned interatomic potentials with the RAFFLE structure-generation framework to construct 13,096 realistic hard carbon models containing up to 4,378 atoms, matching experimentally measured densities, porosities, and sp$^2$/sp$^3$ bonding fractions. Explicit sodium intercalation of representative structures reproduces the characteristic sloping-to-plateau voltage profiles, revealing that capacity increases with decreasing carbon density and increasing porosity. To screen the full library, we train a lightweight neural-network surrogate that predicts capacity directly from the host using frozen universal-potential descriptors augmented by geometric void features. The surrogate identifies high-capacity candidates exceeding 800 mAh g$^{-1}$, which are validated by full intercalation calculations. This scalable framework links hard carbon microstructure to sodium-storage performance and provides atomistic design principles for high-capacity anodes. More broadly, the workflow enables systematic exploration of synthesis-dependent amorphous microstructures, including precursor chemistry, pyrolysis, heteroatom doping, and pore engineering, providing a route toward atomistically informed hard carbon design.
summary: This work addresses the challenge of designing high-capacity hard carbon anodes for sodium-ion batteries by creating a scalable computational workflow. It combines machine-learned potentials with structure generation to build a massive library of realistic carbon models. Crucially, it trains a neural network to predict the sodium storage capacity directly from the structure, allowing for rapid screening and the identification of optimal material designs.
main_problem: To develop a fundamental understanding and systematic design principles for high-capacity hard carbon anodes for sodium-ion batteries, overcoming the limitations of conventional atomistic methods in modeling complex, large-scale, disordered structures.
main_result: The developed framework successfully links hard carbon microstructure (density, porosity, pore morphology) to sodium-storage performance, identifying high-capacity candidates exceeding 800 mAh g-1.
method: The study combines machine-learned interatomic potentials with a structure-generation framework, and then trains a lightweight neural-network surrogate to predict electrochemical capacity directly from the host structure.
model_or_system: The system is hard carbon, a disordered carbon material used as an anode for sodium-ion batteries. The modeling involves generating large libraries of structures using MLIPs and predicting performance using a trained Neural Network (NN) surrogate model.
key_observables: Sodium storage capacity (mAh g-1), voltage profiles (V vs Na/Na+), carbon density, and $sp^3$ bonding fractions.
important_parameters: Porosity, carbon density (especially the threshold $\leq 2 	ext{ g cm}^{-3}$), and the $sp^3$ fraction are key structural descriptors.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the NN surrogate model can accurately predict the complex electrochemical performance based solely on structural descriptors, bypassing computationally prohibitive full intercalation calculations for the entire library.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes reference structural property summaries and validation plots comparing NN predictions to explicit calculations.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of (1) defining the physical problem and limitations of current methods, (2) proposing a combined MLIP/RAFFLE workflow for structure generation, (3) developing and training a NN surrogate model using structural and geometric descriptors, and (4) validating the model by predicting and identifying high-performance candidates.
why_interesting: The application of machine learning (NNs) to predict macroscopic material properties (electrochemical capacity) from complex, disordered atomic structures is a prime example of ML-physics in action, relevant to understanding emergent behavior in disordered systems.
